title: 12 Quantum Cheat Codes to Be Wildly Successful as a Leader
author: The Good Boss
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that conventional leadership advice such as be authentic or listen more is slow and abstract, telling someone to breathe without teaching them to swim. For leaders under pressure he offers twelve compact cheat codes drawn from his own experience. They include never attending a meeting without a goal, replying last in group discussions, scheduling solitude, making fewer but weightier decisions, and treating I am not sure as a skill. Others cover opening 1:1s with an unexpected question, being boringly consistent, using the calendar as strategy, being hard on standards but soft on people, five-minute weekly reviews, leaning into tension, and never scaling bad behavior. The move is to trade inspirational generalities for specific, immediately testable habits.
points: Speaking last in a group discussion avoids anchoring the team and draws out more independent thinking and better ideas.
A leader's calendar is the real statement of priorities, so a weekly ten-minute audit tests whether it reflects what matters.
Saying I do not know signals humility, curiosity and trust, and prompts the team to step up and take ownership.
Being hard on standards but soft on people keeps the bar high while responding to misses with direct, supportive conversation.
The worst behavior a leader tolerates becomes the culture, so toxic high performers must be addressed quickly and directly.
quotes: When you speak first, you (often unintentionally) anchor the discussion. Your team aligns too quickly, and stops thinking independently.
Most leaders are buried under meetings because they’re afraid to say no. But here’s the harsh truth: You get points for making an impact, not for being busy.
Your team doesn’t need a superhero. They need someone they can count on, in good times and bad.
But over these years I’ve realized that saying “I don’t know” is actually a leadership strength. It signals humility, curiosity, and importantly, trust.
If I don’t see time blocked in my calendar for team development, strategic thinking, or customer conversations, they’re not priorities. They’re just slogans.
High standards drive excellence. But how you respond to misses defines your culture. Be direct, honest, and reasonable.
This one is brutal, but true: the worst behavior you tolerate becomes your culture.
